passage:
Keerthana: Hemant, the slides were due at 8. Your part is still blank.
Hemant: wow ok
Hemant: do u know what my week has been like
Keerthana: I know it's been hard, but you said Sunday for sure. Ma'am already asked me.
Hemant: so now everyone's against me. great
Hemant: i try so hard and this is what i get
Keerthana: I'm not against you. I just need the three slides.
Hemant: forget it. tell ma'am it's all my fault since that's what u think
Keerthana: I never said that.
Hemant stared at the screen, thumb hovering. The slides would take forty minutes. But saying sorry felt like admitting he was the kind of person who lets people down, and he couldn't stand that.
Hemant: going offline. dont message me
Keerthana: ok. I'll do your slides.

qa.q: When were the slides due?
qa.a: The slides were due at 8.

qa.q: Why couldn't Hemant bring himself to say sorry?
qa.a: Saying sorry felt like admitting he was someone who lets people down, and his self-image couldn't stand that.

qa.q: What could Hemant have typed while his thumb hovered?
qa.a: He could have written that he was sorry and would send the slides in forty minutes, owning the delay instead of turning it into a story about being attacked.

qa.q: How does Keerthana end up feeling?
qa.a: Keerthana is left tired and unfairly cast as the one who hurt Hemant, and ends up doing extra work after simply asking for the slides.

grounding: A student behind on a group task turns a fair reminder into a story of being attacked, protecting a fragile self-image while Keerthana does the work.

passage:
The tuition teacher's veranda smelled of rain and chalk. Jaya held up a maths notebook, the last six pages brown and wrinkled.
"Maria, you had it yesterday. What happened?"
Maria's face crumpled at once. "Why is it always me? Everyone in this town thinks I'm careless. My amma says it, the bus conductor says it, now you." Tears ran down her cheeks.
The other girls gathered round Maria. Someone patted her back. Someone said, "Jaya, it's only a notebook." Jaya stood alone holding the ruined pages, suddenly the villain.
Maria felt the warmth of the circle. But underneath sat a small, sick feeling. She had spilled her tea on it. Admitting that would make her exactly the careless girl everyone said she was, and she could not bear to be that girl.
Walking home past the rubber trees, she kept seeing Jaya's face.

qa.q: What had happened to the last six pages of Jaya's notebook?
qa.a: The last six pages were brown and wrinkled, because Maria had spilled her tea on it.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as the circle comforted her?
qa.a: She felt warmed by the sympathy, but underneath sat a small, sick feeling because she knew she had spilled the tea.

qa.q: What could Maria do after the walk home past the rubber trees?
qa.a: She could tell Jaya the truth, apologise plainly and offer to rewrite the pages, which would show she can own a mistake without being only the careless girl.

qa.q: How did Jaya experience the scene on the veranda?
qa.a: Jaya went from asking a fair question to standing alone as the villain, which likely felt confusing and unfair.

grounding: A girl who ruined Jaya's notebook turns a fair question into tears about always being blamed, drawing sympathy while knowing she was at fault.

passage:
Saurabh: farida you still have my chem notes. exam is tomorrow
Farida: omg why is everyone attacking me today
Saurabh: i'm not attacking you. i just need the notes
Farida: you don't even know what i'm going through. my mom yelled at me, my phone cracked, and now this
Saurabh: i'm sorry about that. but can you drop them at the gate at 6?
Farida: wow. ok. i guess i'm just the worst person ever
Saurabh: i didn't say that
Farida: everyone always makes me the bad guy
Farida sat on her bed, stomach tight. She had lost the notes two days ago, somewhere between tuition and the bus stop. Admitting that felt like proof she was careless, stupid, a bad friend. Being hurt was easier than being wrong.
Farida: …i lost them. i'm sorry. i'll message the others for photos of theirs
Saurabh: ok. thanks for telling me

qa.q: What time did Saurabh ask Farida to drop the notes at the gate?
qa.a: At 6.

qa.q: Why did Farida keep saying everyone was attacking her?
qa.a: Farida felt ashamed and afraid of being seen as careless, so acting hurt felt easier than admitting she'd lost the notes.

qa.q: What did Farida finally do that helped?
qa.a: She admitted losing the notes, apologised, and offered to get photos of others' notes for Saurabh.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when Farida said she was the worst person ever?
qa.a: Saurabh felt confused and a little stuck, since Saurabh only needed the notes and hadn't blamed Farida.

grounding: It shows a teenager turning a friend's simple request into her own victimhood to avoid admitting fault, from a fragile self-image.

passage:
On the dusty ground behind the village temple, Siddharth was out, run out by a mile, because Ujjwal had called him for a run and then stayed put.
"Why did you call if you weren't coming?" Siddharth said, dusting his knees.
Ujjwal threw down his bat. "Oh, so now it's my fault? Everyone always blames me. Last week the ball in the pond, my fault. The broken window, my fault. Nobody in this team ever sees what I do."
The younger boys went quiet. A few went to pat Ujjwal on the back. Siddharth stood there, holding his helmet, somehow now the bad guy.
Ujjwal walked off to the peepal tree and sat with his back to everyone. His face burned. He had called that run. He knew it. But saying "my mistake" in front of the whole village team felt like being stripped.
It was easier to be the wronged one.

qa.q: Where were the boys playing cricket?
qa.a: On the dusty ground behind the village temple.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal act like the wronged one?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt ashamed and exposed, and admitting the mistake in front of the team felt unbearable, so being wronged was easier.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do to repair the moment?
qa.a: He could go back and say plainly, "My mistake, I called the run," which would end the tension faster than defending himself.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after Ujjwal's outburst?
qa.a: Siddharth felt confused and unfairly blamed, standing there as if he had become the bad guy.

grounding: It shows a teenager turning a complaint about his mistake into sympathy for himself, because being at fault felt unbearable.

passage:
In the library of their Nairobi school, Xin finally asked the question. "Amara, the group project's due tomorrow. Where's your section?"
Amara's eyes filled instantly. "Why are you all ganging up on me? Do you know how hard this week's been? My grandmother's sick, I had netball, and now I'm the villain."
Xin softened. "I'm sorry about your grandmother. I just need to know if it's done."
"You always do this. I try so hard and nobody sees it."
The other two in the group looked at their laptops. Xin felt her own anger turn into guilt, which was strange, because she had done nothing wrong.
Amara stared at the table. She hadn't started the section. She'd forgotten until last night. The idea of saying "I forgot" made her feel like everything good about her would crack.
She wiped her eyes. "Can I have until tonight?"

qa.q: What was due tomorrow?
qa.a: The group project was due tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Amara cry and say everyone was ganging up on her?
qa.a: Amara felt ashamed and scared, because admitting she forgot felt like everything good about her would crack, so being wronged was easier.

qa.q: What could Amara say that would help the group more?
qa.a: She could plainly say "I forgot, I'm sorry, I'll have it done tonight," taking responsibility without the drama.

qa.q: How did Xin feel when Amara turned it around?
qa.a: Xin felt her anger turn into guilt, even though she had done nothing wrong.

grounding: It shows a teenager turning a question about her missing work into sympathy for herself, protecting a fragile self-image.

passage: In the school library during free period, Akash finally said it. "Shalini, the history model is due tomorrow and your part isn't done. We've asked three times." Shalini's eyes filled at once. "Wow. You know I've had the worst week. Nobody ever asks how I am. I always get blamed for everything in every group." The others shifted. Tanu passed her a tissue; someone murmured, "Sorry, Shalu." Akash looked at the table, suddenly the bad guy. Later, walking to the bus alone, Shalini replayed it. She had forgotten the model; that was the truth. But saying "I forgot" had felt like the floor opening under her, like proof she was useless. The tears had come before she chose them. Now everyone was comforting her, and the model still wasn't made. She took out her phone, then put it back, not yet able to type the word sorry.

qa.q: How many times had the group asked about Shalini's part?
qa.a: They had asked three times.

qa.q: Why did saying she forgot feel so hard for Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini feared it was proof of being useless; that shame about being at fault made the tears come before she chose them.

qa.q: What could Shalini do now to repair things?
qa.a: She could message the group, admit she forgot, say sorry plainly and offer to finish her part tonight, instead of turning the complaint into sympathy.

qa.q: How did Akash seem to feel after the others comforted Shalini?
qa.a: Akash seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, looking at the table, as if a fair reminder had made him the bad guy.

grounding: Shows a teenager turning a fair complaint into sympathy for herself because being at fault feels unbearable.
